content:
Facts: Following an intestate succession, the surviving spouse and children sought judicial division of a complex estate mainly consisting of co-owned real estate. The defendants raised procedural objections (mandatory mediation, partial division), counterclaimed for simulation of a prior sale, collation of alleged donations, suspension of division, and compensation for exclusive occupation of inherited assets.
Legal framework
Articles 581, 720, 726–727, 1111, 737 ICC on intestate succession, division of inheritance, inconvenient divisibility, cash adjustments, suspension of division, and collation; Legislative Decree 28/2010 on mandatory mediation; Articles 167 and 183 CPC on assertive preclusions; principles on valuation of assets at the time of division, simulation, rendering of accounts, and civil fruits between co-heirs.
Interpretative issue
Whether the action for division was admissible despite objections relating to mediation and alleged partiality of the claim; under what conditions a judicial suspension of division may be ordered; whether a counterclaim for simulation or collation is admissible and sufficiently proven; how indivisible inherited real estate should be allocated; and whether a co-heir in exclusive possession owes compensation for civil fruits to the others.
Principle applied
In inheritance division proceedings, mandatory mediation is satisfied if the procedure is initiated and concluded before the first hearing, irrespective of the timing of service of the writ of summons. The division must concern the entire estate actually existing at the opening of the succession, and objections of partial division are inadmissible absent specific proof of omitted assets. Judicial suspension of division under Article 1111 ICC requires serious prejudice to the collective interest of all co-heirs, not to an individual position. Counterclaims for simulation and collation, constituting strict exceptions, are subject to assertive and evidentiary preclusions and must be timely raised and strictly proven. Where inherited assets are inconveniently divisible under Article 720 ICC, the judge may allocate them to one or more co-heirs with cash adjustments, exercising broad discretionary power guided by criteria of expediency and proportionality. Assets must be valued at their actual market value at the time of division, regardless of their formal cadastral classification. A co-heir who has enjoyed exclusive possession of inherited property is obliged, upon division, to render account and to pay the other co-heirs their pro rata share of the civil fruits accrued from the opening of the succession, irrespective of good or bad faith.
